turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: Hi, thanks for making time today. Before I get into anything about us, can I ask what's prompting you to even take this call right now?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Sure, happy to share. We've had a rough few months with caregiver call-offs and family complaints about visit consistency, and honestly I'm tired of playing detective every time a client's daughter calls asking why the visit was twelve minutes short.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That's a big one. How many caregivers and clients are you running right now, roughly?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: We're at about 85 caregivers and 140 active clients across two counties. We grew fast the last two years, and our systems didn't really grow with us.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: Got it. And when a shortfall happens — like that twelve-minute example — how do you even find out? Family complaint, or do you catch it internally first?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Almost always the family catches it before we do. Our EVV system just tells us clock-in and clock-out times, it doesn't tell us what actually happened in the home. So we're reactive, not proactive, and that's damaging trust with our referral sources.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That reactive position is expensive in a few ways. Can I ask — what's your caregiver turnover looking like this year, and do you have a sense of average length of stay per client?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Turnover's brutal, honestly north of 65% annually, which is close to industry norm but still painful. Average length of stay is maybe 14 months, and I know if we lost fewer clients to "we don't feel comfortable anymore" moments, that number would climb.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That connects directly to what I wanted to walk through today. Sensi.AI puts a passive AI listening layer into the home — through a device already there, no wearables, no cameras — and it flags things like falls, unusual silence, medication conversations, agitation, wandering risk, that kind of signal, in real time. Agencies using it see caregivers get about 35% more billable hours because supervisors stop spending time on manual spot-checks and can actually staff and sell more hours instead. Does that kind of visibility problem resonate with what you're describing?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: It does, actually — a lot of our office coordinators' time goes to babysitting compliance instead of business development. If we could reclaim even half of that, we could be pushing more hours into the field instead of admin overhead.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: Makes sense. When you think about length of stay — the families who cancel service — what's usually the actual trigger, in your experience?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Usually it's a trust breakdown. A fall nobody reported until the next shift, or the caregiver on their phone the whole visit, or medication not given on time and nobody flags it. Families don't leave because care is bad exactly — they leave because they stop believing they'd hear about it if something went wrong.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That's exactly the gap this closes. Every visit gets an automated summary the family and office can see — engagement level, safety flags, wellness trends over time — so instead of families finding out after the fact, your coordinators are proactively calling to say "hey, we noticed mom seemed more withdrawn this week, let's check in." Agencies using that proactive-outreach motion are converting more of their assessments into long-term clients too — we're seeing about 2.6x higher conversion when families see that kind of transparency during the sales process itself.

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: That's interesting because our intake conversion has actually been a struggle — families shop around and a lot of them just don't come back after the initial assessment. If we had something concrete to show them about how care is monitored, that could be a real differentiator in a crowded market.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: How many assessments are you running a month right now, roughly, and what's your close rate?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: We're doing maybe 30 assessments a month and closing around 40%. If that number moved even a little with something like this, it'd be a meaningful revenue swing for us, not just a nice-to-have.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That tracks with what we typically see. On the turnover side — since caregivers are also flagged as being on their phones or not engaged — how do you think your team would react to that kind of oversight? Sometimes that's the part owners worry about.

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Good caregivers usually don't mind it once they understand it's protecting them too — if there's a fall and it's not their fault, the record actually backs them up instead of it becoming a he-said-she-said with the family. It's really the mediocre performers who'll push back, and honestly I don't mind losing a few of those if it means we retain the good ones and protect ourselves legally.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That's a healthy way to think about it — it tends to work as a retention tool for your best people, not a punishment system. Given everything you've described — the reactive complaints, the 65% turnover, the assessment conversion gap — where does solving this sit on your priority list for this quarter?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Honestly it's near the top. We're about to head into our slow season for new referrals, so if there's a way to shore up retention and improve our close rate before Q1 hiring season hits, I'd rather move on it now than wait.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That's good timing on our end too. What I'd suggest next is a working session with your ops lead and whoever runs your intake process — I'll bring our clinical outcomes data and we can map it against your specific numbers, turnover, assessment volume, average length of stay, and build a real ROI picture instead of a generic one. Would Thursday at 2pm work, or does early next week work better for your team's schedules?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Thursday at 2 should work — let me just loop in my operations director since she owns the day-to-day and would need to be in that conversation anyway.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: Perfect, send me her email after this and I'll get a calendar invite out today with a short agenda so nobody's walking in cold. One more thing before we wrap — is there a specific incident or complaint from the last few months that, if we solved nothing else, would make this an easy yes for you?

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Yeah, actually — we had a fall two months ago that wasn't reported for almost four hours, and the family found out from the hospital before we even called them. That one cost us the client and it still keeps me up at night. If this platform would've caught that in real time, that alone justifies the conversation.

turns.speaker: Rep
turns.text: That's precisely the scenario this is built to prevent, and I'll bring a case study Thursday from an agency that had almost that exact situation so you can see how it played out differently on their end. I'll get that invite over now — talk soon.

turns.speaker: Prospect
turns.text: Sounds good, looking forward to it.
